claim: Each Drosophila muscle is seeded by one Founder Cell issued from terminal division of a Progenitor Cell (PC).
source: Each Drosophila muscle is seeded by one Founder Cell issued from terminal division of a Progenitor Cell (PC).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of Drosophila muscle development.

claim: Muscle identity reflects the expression by each PC of a specific combination of identity Transcription Factors (iTFs).
source: Muscle identity reflects the expression by each PC of a specific combination of identity Transcription Factors (iTFs).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field and is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sequential emergence of several PCs at the same position raised the question of how developmental time controlled muscle identity.
source: Sequential emergence of several PCs at the same position raised the question of how developmental time controlled muscle identity.
evidence: This represents the research question motivating the study.

claim: Anterior Open (Aop) controls PC birth time.
source: Here, we identified roles of Anterior Open and ETS domain lacking in controlling PC birth time
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing altered PC selection timing in aop mutants.

claim: ETS domain lacking (Edl) controls PC birth time.
source: Here, we identified roles of Anterior Open and ETS domain lacking in controlling PC birth time
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing altered PC selection timing in edl mutants.

claim: Eyes absent (Eya) specifies PC identity.
source: Here, we identified roles of Anterior Open and ETS domain lacking in controlling PC birth time and Eyes absent, No Ocelli, and Sine oculis in specifying PC identity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing muscle identity defects in eya mutants.

claim: No Ocelli (Noc) specifies PC identity.
source: Here, we identified roles of Anterior Open and ETS domain lacking in controlling PC birth time and Eyes absent, No Ocelli, and Sine oculis in specifying PC identity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing muscle identity defects in noc mutants.

claim: Sine oculis (So) specifies PC identity.
source: Here, we identified roles of Anterior Open and ETS domain lacking in controlling PC birth time and Eyes absent, No Ocelli, and Sine oculis in specifying PC identity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing muscle identity defects in so mutants.

claim: The Drosophila larva has 30 different muscles in each hemi-segment.
source: The development of the complex architecture of the body wall musculature of the Drosophila larva – 30 different muscles in each hemi-segment (Bate, 1993)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bate, 1993.

claim: Each muscle is a single multinucleated fiber built by fusion of a Founder Cell (FC) with fusion competent myoblasts (FCMs).
source: Each muscle is a single multinucleated fiber built by fusion of a Founder Cell (FC) with fusion competent myoblasts (FCMs).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of Drosophila muscle development.

claim: Muscle identity - orientation, shape, size, attachment sites - reflects the expression by each FC of a specific combination of identity Transcription Factors (iTFs).
source: Muscle identity - orientation, shape, size, attachment sites - reflects the expression by each FC of a specific combination of identity Transcription Factors (iTFs).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field and is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Establishment of the FC iTF code starts with activation of specific muscle iTFs, in response to positional information from the ectoderm which defines equivalence groups of myoblasts within each segment, called promuscular clusters (PMCs).
source: Establishment of the FC iTF code starts with activation of specific muscle iTFs, in response to positional information from the ectoderm which defines equivalence groups of myoblasts within each segment, called promuscular clusters (PMCs) (Carmena et al., 1995; Baylies et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carmena et al., 1995 and Baylies et al., 1998.

claim: The second step is the selection of progenitor cells (PCs) from each PMC, via interplay between Ras signaling and Notch (N)/Delta-mediated lateral inhibition, the unselected myoblasts becoming FCMs.
source: The second step is the selection of progenitor cells (PCs) from each PMC, via interplay between Ras signaling and Notch (N)/Delta-mediated lateral inhibition, the unselected myoblasts becoming FCMs (Carmena et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carmena et al., 2002.

claim: The third step is the asymmetric division of each PC into two FCs or, in some cases, one FC and one adult muscle precursor cell (AMP) or pericardial cell.
source: The third step is the asymmetric division of each PC into two FCs or, in some cases, one FC and one adult muscle precursor cell (AMP) or pericardial cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of Drosophila muscle development.

claim: Asymmetric division leads to maintaining expression of some iTFs in one FC and their repression by N signaling in the sibling cell, thereby contributing to muscle lineage diversity.
source: Asymmetric division leads to maintaining expression of some iTFs in one FC and their repression by N signaling in the sibling cell, thereby contributing to muscle lineage diversity (Ruiz-Gomez et al., 1997; Carmena et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ruiz-Gomez et al., 1997 and Carmena et al., 1998.

claim: Specification of two nearby Even-skipped (Eve) expressing PCs was sequential.
source: Interestingly, pioneering studies showed that specification of two nearby Even-skipped (Eve) expressing PCs was sequential (Buff et al., 1998; Halfon et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Buff et al., 1998 and Halfon et al., 2000.

claim: Four PCs, at the origin of one dorsal muscle (DA2) and one AMP, and the 6 dorso-lateral (DL) muscles, DA3, DO3, DO4, DO5, DT1, and LL1, are serially selected from a PMC expressing Collier (Col/Kn, Early B-Cell Factor (EBF) in vertebrates).
source: We have previously shown that four PCs, at the origin of one dorsal muscle (DA2) and one AMP, and the 6 dorso-lateral (DL) muscles, DA3, DO3, DO4, DO5, DT1, and LL1, are serially selected from a PMC expressing Collier (Col/Kn, Early B-Cell Factor (EBF) in vertebrates (Daburon et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Daburon et al., 2008.

claim: The DA2/AMP, DA3/DO5 and LL1/DO4 PCs are sequentially selected at roughly identical positions in thoracic and abdominal segments.
source: More precisely, the DA2/AMP, DA3/DO5 and LL1/DO4 PCs are sequentially selected at roughly identical positions in thoracic and abdominal segments, while the DO3/DT1 PC is selected at a slightly posterior position and only in abdominal segments (Boukhatmi et al., 2012; Enriquez et al., 2012; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boukhatmi et al., 2012 and Enriquez et al., 2012, and by Figure 1A.

claim: The DO3/DT1 PC is selected at a slightly posterior position and only in abdominal segments.
source: More precisely, the DA2/AMP, DA3/DO5 and LL1/DO4 PCs are sequentially selected at roughly identical positions in thoracic and abdominal segments, while the DO3/DT1 PC is selected at a slightly posterior position and only in abdominal segments (Boukhatmi et al., 2012; Enriquez et al., 2012; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boukhatmi et al., 2012 and Enriquez et al., 2012, and by Figure 1A.

claim: col transcription is only maintained in the DA3 muscle beyond the PC step.
source: Beyond the PC step, col transcription is only maintained in the DA3 muscle (Crozatier and Vincent, 1999)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Crozatier and Vincent, 1999.

claim: Krüppel (Kr) is expressed in the LL1 lineage.
source: while other iTFs, the C2H2 zinc finger protein Krüppel (Kr), the homeodomain protein S59 (vertebrate NKx1.1) and the Lim-homeodomain protein Tailup (Tup/Islet1) are expressed in the LL1, DT1 and DA2 lineages, respectively (Dohrmann et al., 1990; Ruiz Gomez and Bate, 1997; Boukhatmi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dohrmann et al., 1990; Ruiz Gomez and Bate, 1997; Boukhatmi et al., 2012.

claim: S59 is expressed in the DT1 lineage.
source: while other iTFs, the C2H2 zinc finger protein Krüppel (Kr), the homeodomain protein S59 (vertebrate NKx1.1) and the Lim-homeodomain protein Tailup (Tup/Islet1) are expressed in the LL1, DT1 and DA2 lineages, respectively (Dohrmann et al., 1990; Ruiz Gomez and Bate, 1997; Boukhatmi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dohrmann et al., 1990; Ruiz Gomez and Bate, 1997; Boukhatmi et al., 2012.

claim: Tailup (Tup/Islet1) is expressed in the DA2 lineage.
source: while other iTFs, the C2H2 zinc finger protein Krüppel (Kr), the homeodomain protein S59 (vertebrate NKx1.1) and the Lim-homeodomain protein Tailup (Tup/Islet1) are expressed in the LL1, DT1 and DA2 lineages, respectively (Dohrmann et al., 1990; Ruiz Gomez and Bate, 1997; Boukhatmi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dohrmann et al., 1990; Ruiz Gomez and Bate, 1997; Boukhatmi et al., 2012.

claim: Tup expression leads to col repression in the DA2/AMP PC, thereby distinguishing between DA2 and DA3 identities.
source: The discovery that Tup expression led to col repression in the DA2/AMP PC, thereby distinguishing between DA2 and DA3 identities, provided a first insight into this question.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: The time lag between DA2/AMP and DA3/DO5 PC selection coincides with the period of dorsal regression of Tinman (Tin; vertebrate Nkx2.5) expression.
source: We indeed found that the time lag between DA2/AMP and DA3/DO5 PC selection coincides with the period of dorsal regression of Tinman (Tin; vertebrate Nkx2.5) expression (Johnson et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Johnson et al., 2011.

claim: Only the first-born DA2 PC inherits Tin levels above the threshold required for activation of tup and imposing a DA2 fate.
source: such that only the first-born DA2 PC inherits Tin levels above the threshold required for activation of tup and imposing a DA2 fate.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work and is supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: A systematic deficiency screen of the second chromosome was performed to identify new muscle TFs.
source: Here, we identified several new muscle TFs, starting from a systematic deficiency screen of the second chromosome, i.e., roughly 40% of the Drosophila genome.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: No Ocelli (Noc) is a NET family zinc finger protein.
source: We describe the roles of No Ocelli (Noc), a NET family zinc finger protein (Cheah et al., 1994)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cheah et al., 1994.

claim: Sine oculis (So) is a member of the Six family of homeodomain proteins.
source: Sine oculis (So), a member of the Six family of homeodomain proteins (Cheyette et al., 1994; Serikaku and O'Tousa, 1994; Kenyon et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cheyette et al., 1994; Serikaku and O'Tousa, 1994; Kenyon et al., 2005.

claim: Edl is a co-factor.
source: and the co-factor ETS domain lacking Edl (Baker et al., 2001; Yamada et al., 2003; Qiao et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baker et al., 2001; Yamada et al., 2003; Qiao et al., 2006.

claim: Eyes-absent (Eya) is a partner of Six proteins.
source: Eyes-absent (Eya), a partner of Six proteins (Pignoni et al., 1997)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pignoni et al., 1997.

claim: Anterior open (Aop) is an Ets-domain transcription repressor.
source: Anterior open (Aop), an Ets-domain transcription repressor (Rebay and Rubin, 1995; Xu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rebay and Rubin, 1995 and Xu et al., 2000.

claim: aop and edl control the temporal sequence of DL PC selections.
source: Analysis of the aop, edl, eya, noc and so muscle mutant phenotypes and time windows of transcription, combined with col transcription in the different mutant contexts, revealed a cascade of regulations including coherent and incoherent feed-forward loops, which link PC selection time to muscle identity. aop and edl control the temporal sequence of DL PC selections
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing altered PC selection timing in aop and edl mutants.

claim: eya is required in PCs for maintaining iTF transcription.
source: eya is required in PCs for maintaining iTF transcription
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing loss of iTF expression in eya mutants.

claim: so is deployed at the FC step.
source: while so and one eya-specific isoform are deployed at the FC step.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing so expression and function at the FC stage.

claim: One eya-specific isoform is deployed at the FC step.
source: while so and one eya-specific isoform are deployed at the FC step.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing eya-RB expression at the FC stage.

claim: noc regulates expression of other iTFs, at the PC or FC step, depending upon the muscle lineage.
source: Finally, noc regulates expression of other iTFs, at the PC or FC step, depending upon the muscle lineage.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing lineage-specific effects of noc on iTF expression.

claim: A collection of 389 overlapping deficiencies was screened, each deleting between 10 and 15 genes, and together covering about 80% of the Drosophila second chromosome.
source: In order to identify new muscle identity genes, we screened a collection of 389 overlapping deficiencies, each deleting between 10 and 15 genes, and together covering about 80% of the Drosophila second chromosome (Chanut-Delalande et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and is supported by a citation to Chanut-Delalande et al., 2014.

claim: 36 chromosomal deficiencies were retained for further analysis based on DA3 phenotypes.
source: 36 were retained (Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: The observed DA3 phenotypes were divided into two broad classes: Class 1 (generic myogenesis defects) and Class 2 (muscle identity defects).
source: The observed DA3 phenotypes were divided into two broad classes (Figure 1C): Class 1: Decreased number or abnormal repartition of nuclei (Figure 1E–F compare to Figure 1D); Class 2: Abnormal DA3 orientation and/or either loss of Col expression or ectopic Col expression in additional muscles (Figure 1G–I compare to Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1C-I.

claim: From a total of 36 different chromosomal regions, 9 genes out of 10 regions were identified as linked to generic defects and 15 genes in 14 regions were linked to identity defects.
source: From a total of 36 different chromosomal regions, we identified 9 genes out of 10 regions linked to generic defects and 15 genes in 14 regions linked to identity defects (Figure 1J,K and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1J,K and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: Seven of the nine genes in the generic class encode cytoskeletal or membrane-associated proteins with an already well-known role in either myoblast fusion or nuclei repartition in muscle syncitia.
source: Seven of the nine genes in the generic class encode cytoskeletal or membrane-associated proteins with an already well-known role in either myoblast fusion or nuclei repartition in muscle syncitia, validating our screen (Figure 1J; Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1J and a citation to Kim et al., 2015.

claim: sin3A is a chromatin binding protein present in transcription repressor complexes, also required for a normal pattern of myoblast fusions.
source: The eigth gene is sin3A, a chromatin binding protein present in transcription repressor complexes, also required for a normal pattern of myoblast fusions (Dobi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dobi et al., 2014.

claim: basigin (bsg) is a predicted igG family plasma membrane protein, interacting with integrin.
source: The 9th gene is basigin (bsg), a predicted igG family plasma membrane protein, interacting with integrin (Curtin et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Curtin et al., 2005.

claim: Among the 15 genes associated with identity phenotypes, six encoded components of either the N or Robo/Slit signaling pathways.
source: Among the 15 genes associated with identity phenotypes (Figure 1K), six encoded components of either the N or Robo/Slit signaling pathways, two pathways previously implicated at different steps of DA3 muscle formation (Crozatier and Vincent, 1999; Ordan et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1K and citations to Crozatier and Vincent, 1999 and Ordan et al., 2015.

claim: Four genes associated with identity phenotypes encoded components of the EGF-R signaling pathway: spitz (spi), Star (S), aop, and edl.
source: Four other encoded components of the EGF-R signaling pathway: spitz (spi), Star (S), aop (also called yan; Flybase FBgn 000097), and edl (also called mae; Flybase FBgn0023214)
evidence: This is a finding from the screen.

claim: A deficiency removing both mesodermal FGFs, Thisbe and Pyramus, did not show a DA3 phenotype.
source: while a deficiency (Df(2R)BSC259) removing both mesodermal FGFs, Thisbe and Pyramus, (Stathopoulos et al., 2004) did not show a DA3 phenotype.
evidence: This is a finding from the screen and is supported by a citation to Stathopoulos et al., 2004.

claim: A complete lack of DA3, DO5, DO4 and LL1 muscles in mutants for either spi or Star confirmed the central role of Epidermal Growth Factor-Receptor (EGF-R) signaling in specification of these DL muscles.
source: A complete lack of DA3, DO5, DO4 and LL1 muscles in mutants for either spi (spiIIA), the EGF-R signal, or Star (SIIN), a chaperone protein required for Spi processing (Heberlein and Rubin, 1991), confirmed the central role of Epidermal Growth Factor-Receptor (EGF-R) signaling in specification of these DL muscles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Heberlein and Rubin, 1991.

claim: Seven identity genes encoded transcriptional regulators, and potentially, new muscle iTFs: aop, edl, eya, noc, so, spalt major (salm) and tup.
source: Seven identity genes encoded transcriptional regulators, and potentially, new muscle iTFs: aop, edl, eya, noc, so, spalt major (salm) and tup (Figures 1K and 2A–F).
evidence: This is supported by Figures 1K and 2A–F.

claim: The Ets-domain transcription activator Pointed (Pnt), and transcription repressor Aop/Yan promoted and inhibited the formation of Eve-expressing dorsal PCs, respectively, downstream of EGF-R signaling.
source: Previous studies showed that the Ets-domain transcription activator Pointed (Pnt), and transcription repressor Aop/Yan (Xu et al., 2000; Rebay and Rubin, 1995), promoted and inhibited the formation of Eve-expressing dorsal PCs, respectively, downstream of EGF-R signaling (Halfon et al., 2000; Carmena et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2000; Rebay and Rubin, 1995; Halfon et al., 2000; Carmena et al., 2002.

claim: Drosophila Six4 and So are orthologous to Six proteins which interact with Eya in mouse myogenic progenitors.
source: Drosophila Six4 and So are orthologous to Six proteins which interact with Eya in mouse myogenic progenitors (Heanue et al., 1999; Relaix et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Heanue et al., 1999 and Relaix et al., 2013.

claim: eya was proposed to interact with Six4 in Drosophila somatic muscle development, both genes showing similar expression patterns.
source: eya was proposed to interact with Six4 in Drosophila somatic muscle development, both genes showing similar expression patterns (Clark et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clark et al., 2006 and Liu et al., 2009.

claim: In aop mutants, the DA3 muscle(s) was misshapen in 2/3 of segments (n = 123).
source: In aop mutants, the DA3 muscle(s) was misshapen in 2/3 of segments (n = 123), with cases of DA3 to DA2 transformation (DA3>DA2; Figure 2B, Figure 2— figure supplement 2, Video 2 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Video 2 and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: In aop mutants, the DT1 and LL1 muscles were malformed in 40% segments.
source: The DT1 and LL1 muscles were also malformed in 40% segments (in 48/123 and 47/123 segments, respectively)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from the manuscript.

claim: In aop mutants, lateral and ventral muscles were severely disorganized.
source: and lateral and ventral muscles were severely disorganized.
evidence: This is an observation from the mutant analysis.

claim: In aop mutants, the DA2 muscle was unaffected.
source: The DA2 muscle was unaffected (Figure 2H—and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2H and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: In edl mutants, a second Col-expressing muscle was observed in some segments, sometimes associated with morphological change suggestive of DA2>DA3 transformation.
source: In edl mutants, a second Col-expressing muscle was observed in some segments, sometimes associated with morphological change suggestive of DA2>DA3 transformation (Figure 2C,I, Figure 2— figure supplement 2, Video 3 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2C,I, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Video 3 and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: In edl mutants, the DT1 muscle was either absent or too de-structured to be assigned specific identities (in 61/124 segments).
source: The DT1 muscle was either absent or too de-structured to be assigned specific identities (in 61/124 segments; Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2I and quantitative data.

claim: In eya mutants, DA3 Col expression was lost, a loss already observed at the PC stage.
source: In eya mutants, DA3 Col expression was lost, a loss already observed at the PC stage (Figure 2D,J).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2D,J.

claim: In eya mutants, the DL muscle pattern was severely disorganized in most of segments.
source: Consistent with loss of Col expression early during muscle specification, the DL muscle pattern was severely disorganized in most of segments.
evidence: This is an observation from the mutant analysis.

claim: In eya mutants, the LL1 was absent or oriented like DA3 (in 129/140 segments).
source: The LL1 was absent or oriented like DA3 (in 129/140 segments; Figure 2J, Figure 2— figure supplement 2, Video 4 and Figure 2—source data 1) a phenotype already observed in col mutant embryos (Enriquez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2J, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Video 4, Figure 2—source data 1, and a citation to Enriquez et al., 2012.

claim: In eya mutants, dorsal muscles and DT1 appeared normal.
source: Conversely, dorsal muscles and DT1 appeared normal (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2J.

claim: noc mutant embryos lacked DA3 Col expression at stage 15.
source: noc mutant embryos also lacked DA3 Col expression at stage 15 (Figure 2E,K and Figure 2, Figure 2— figure supplement 2, Video 5 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2E,K, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Video 5 and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: In noc mutants, Col expression was detected at the PC stage.
source: Contrary to eya mutants, however, Col expression was detected at the PC stage (insets in Figure 2E), indicating a role of noc in maintenance of Col expression in the DA3 lineage.
evidence: This is supported by insets in Figure 2E.

claim: In noc mutants, the DA3 could orient like a DT1 in most segments, indicating a DA3>DT1 identity shift resulting in DT1 duplication.
source: colLCRM-moeGFP expression further revealed that the DA3 could orient like a DT1 in most segments, indicating a DA3>DT1 identity shift resulting in DT1 duplication (Figure 2Q and and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2Q and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: In so mutants, Col ectopic expression was specifically observed in DO5.
source: In so mutants, Col ectopic expression was specifically observed in DO5 (Figure 2F,L, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Video 6, and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2F,L, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Video 6, and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: In so mutants, colLCRM-moeGFP expression confirmed col ectopic expression in the DO5 muscle and its DA3-like orientation in a fraction of segments, indicating a partial DO5>DA3 identity shift in 79/116 segments.
source: colLCRM-moeGFP expression both confirmed col ectopic expression in the DO5 muscle and its DA3-like orientation in a fraction of segments (Figure 2R, arrowhead, indicating a partial DO5>DA3 identity shift in 79/116 segments (Figure 2F,L and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2R, Figure 2F,L and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: High-resolution 3-D analyses allow unambiguous identification of the DA2/AMP and DL PCs and the derived DA2, DA3 and DO5 FCs and AMP.
source: High-resolution 3-D analyses allow us to unambiguously identify the DA2/AMP and DL PCs and the derived DA2, DA3 and DO5 FCs and AMP (Enriquez et al., 2012; Figure 1A and Figure 3— figure supplement 1, Video 7).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Enriquez et al., 2012, Figure 1A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Video 7.

claim: In early stage 10 embryos, the first selected, DA2/AMP PC is recognizable as a large apical cell, expressing high Nau levels.
source: In early stage 10 embryos, the first selected, DA2/AMP PC is recognizable as a large apical cell, expressing high Nau levels (Figure 3B,B').
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3B,B'.

claim: At stage 11, after the DA2/AMP PC has divided, the DA3/DO5 PC is observed, adjacent to the DA2 FC.
source: At stage 11, after the DA2/AMP PC has divided, the DA3/DO5 PC is observed, adjacent to the DA2 FC (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3C.

claim: 3-D analyses revealed previously undescribed, low level Nau expression in two or three cells surrounding each PC being selected.
source: 3-D analyses also revealed previously undescribed, low level Nau expression in two or three cells surrounding each PC being selected (Figure 3B,F; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3B,F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: This Nau expression pattern was reminiscent of subgroups of PMCs cells displaying higher level dpMAPK (di-phospho mitogen-associated protein kinase), diagnostic of EGFR activity.
source: This Nau expression pattern was reminiscent of subgroups of PMCs cells displaying higher level dpMAPK (di-phospho mitogen-associated protein kinase), diagnostic of EGFR activity (Carmena et al., 1998, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carmena et al., 1998, 2002.

claim: Double staining confirmed that the Nau and dpMAPK patterns overlap, revealing that low level Nau expression corresponds to cells transitioning from PMC to PC, before reaching high level in selected PCs.
source: Double staining confirmed that the Nau and dpMAPK patterns overlap, revealing that low level Nau expression corresponds to cells transitioning from PMC to PC, before reaching high level in selected PCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: FISH experiments indicated aop transcription in Col PMC cells but not PCs.
source: FISH experiments indicated aop transcription in Col PMC cells (Figure 3B), but not PCs (Figure 3B'–E)
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3B and Figure 3B'–E.

claim: aop repression during the PC selection process is consistent with a role in promoting FCM fate.
source: indicating its repression during the PC selection process, consistent with a role in promoting FCM fate (Carmena et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carmena et al., 2002 and is an inference from the expression data.

claim: aop is a target of the FCM TF Lameduck.
source: and being a target of the FCM TF Lameduck (Ciglar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ciglar et al., 2014.

claim: edl transcription was not detected in PMC cells, but in PCs and the dorsal AMP and DA3 FC.
source: Conversely, edl transcription was not detected in PMC cells, but in PCs and the dorsal AMP and DA3 FC (Figure 3F–I).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3F–I.

claim: aop and edl show sequential, complementary transcription patterns.
source: Thus aop and edl show sequential, complementary transcription patterns.
evidence: This is an inference from the expression data presented.

claim: In stage 10 aop mutant embryos, col transcription was detected in PMC cells as in wt.
source: In stage 10 aop mutant embryos, col transcription was detected in PMC cells as in wt (Figure 3P,S and V).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3P,S and V.

claim: In aop mutants, a significantly increased number of cells expressing low Nau level revealed that aop down-regulation of EGF-R signaling was required to restrict Nau expression to PMC cells primed to become PCs.
source: However, a significantly increased number of cells expressing low Nau level revealed that aop down-regulation of EGF-R signaling was required to restrict Nau expression to PMC cells primed to become PCs (Figure 3P,S,V).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3P,S,V and quantitative analysis.

claim: 3-D reconstructions confirmed the presence of two apical cells expressing high Nau Level in aop mutants (21/27 PMCs with 2, and 6/27 with 1 apical PC), when only the DA2/AMP PC was observed in wt (30/35 PMC with 1 apical PC and 5/35 with no apical PC).
source: Furthermore, 3-D reconstructions confirmed the presence of two apical cells expressing high Nau Level (21/27 PMCs with 2, and 6/27 with 1 apical PC), when only the DA2/AMP PC was observed in wt (30/35 PMC with 1 apical PC and 5/35 with no apical PC; Figure 3J,L).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3J,L and quantitative data.

claim: Concomitant, early selection of two PCs in aop embryos prefigures the DA3>DA2 transformation.
source: Thus, concomitant, early selection of two PCs in aop embryos prefigures the DA3>DA2 transformation (Figure 2T).
evidence: This is an inference from the data, supported by Figure 2T.

claim: In edl mutant embryos, no high Nau-expressing apical cell was observed at stage 10 (30/37 segments), when the DA2/AMP PC is selected in wt embryos.
source: Conversely, in edl mutant embryos, no high Nau-expressing apical cell was observed at stage 10 (30/37 segments), when the DA2/AMP PC is selected in wt embryos.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from the manuscript.

claim: In edl mutants, three to four small low Nau-positive cells remained embedded in the Col PMC.
source: Rather, three to four small low Nau-positive cells remained embedded in the Col PMC (Figure 3N compare with Figure 3J) (Figure 3O compare to Figure 3K) both of which transcribed col (Figure 3T compare with Figure 3Q).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3N,O,T,Q.

source: Multiple levels of cross-regulation (Figure 7) could provide robustness to the final muscle pattern.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data, supported by Figure 7.

claim: Nkx2.5, Eya, Six1, Islet1, Col/Ebf and MyoD, are core components of transcriptional regulatory networks controlling the development of pharyngeal/facial muscles originating from the cardio-pharyngeal territory in chordates.
source: While a function of Nolz proteins in the mesoderm remains to be investigated, Nkx2.5, Eya, Six1, Islet1, Col/Ebf and MyoD, are core components of transcriptional regulatory networks controlling the development of pharyngeal/facial muscles originating from the cardio-pharyngeal territory in chordates.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: These conserved mesodermal TFs could combinatorically control muscle regional diversity in vertebrates.
source: Our data raise the possibility that these conserved mesodermal TFs could combinatorically control muscle regional diversity in vertebrates, attested by human muscular dystrophies (Emery, 2002). but whose molecular basis remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and supported by a citation to Emery, 2002.

claim: It is reasonable to speculate that these TFs have been co-opted in different wirings during evolution to generate the muscle lineage diversity found in the animal kingdom.
source: It is reasonable to speculate that these TFs have been co-opted in different wirings during evolution to generate the muscle lineage diversity found in the animal kingdom.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and evolutionary considerations.
